chapters.relation: Hagberg argues that Grant Gee's documentary Patience (After Sebald) achieves a truthful portrait of W. G. Sebald not by static correspondence but by enacting his shifting, connection-making sensibility, as displayed in The Rings of Saturn. He deploys Wittgenstein's remarks on aspect-perception and 'seeing-as' (the duck-rabbit, the 'lighting up of an aspect') to show that perception is always already inflected by imagination, memory and language-games, dismantling the empiricist picture of Locke, Hume and Berkeley in which brute sensation precedes reflection. Borges's 'The Garden of Forking Paths' and 'Tlon, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius' supply the model of a Heraclitean flux of forking, mind-dependent connections, and the film's darkroom-like fading images and layered soundtrack are read as mimetically faithful to how a human sensibility perceives and remembers.

Warren draws on Chantal Akerman's own remark that she makes no distinction between documentary and fiction ('they are all just films') to argue that every Akerman work fuses observation and transfiguration, extension and 'intension.' Reading Je tu il elle, Jeanne Dielman, News from Home and From the Other Side, he shows how documentation of the mundane (Delphine Seyrig molding meatloaf, the Mexico border fence as a blank projection screen) is always already a fashioning, so the real becomes itself only through being made into film. He links the strange, surreal wonder Akerman's border and night-train images provoke to Heidegger's pre-Socratic question of Being ('How is it that we are?') and to a phenomenological attentiveness to the everyday, following Rancière and Cavell on film's double nature.

Linda Williams analyzes Michelle Citron's What You Take for Granted, a feminist film that inhabits the gray zone between documentary and fiction by having actors impersonate real women workers (a truck driver, a doctor, a welder) entering male-dominated trades. She argues the film exposes the price women pay to be admitted to a male world of work structured by an absent, idealized-and-vilified paternal authority, mirroring the absent-mother structure of Citron's earlier Daughter Rite. By blending polished pseudo-documentary interviews with an improvised cinema-verite fiction of Anna and Dianna's friendship, the film interrogates the process of representation itself and shows how documentary 'truth' about women's typical experience is itself a fictional shaping.

Hoffman reads Sarah Polley's Stories We Tell and Joshua Oppenheimer's The Act of Killing through Kierkegaard's account of indirect communication and 'deceiving into the truth.' Like the Socratic maieutic teacher who removes his authority and lets pupils reach their own conclusions, both directors withhold voice-of-God assertion and instead present multiple, conflicting, sometimes ethically monstrous storytellers, indulging their delusions to expose them. Polley stages fake Super-8 home movies and rival accounts of her mother and paternity so that truth becomes subjective appropriation rather than objective fact; Oppenheimer lets Indonesian genocide perpetrators reenact their killings as Hollywood fantasies until Anwar Congo is 'deceived' into his own broken self-awareness, indicting the regime that still celebrates him.

LaRocca argues that Casey Affleck's I'm Still Here, in which Joaquin Phoenix faked a drug-addled retirement and hip-hop career, is best understood as a 'hoax-verite' whose collapse of the boundary between real and represented turns it into a Baudrillardian simulacrum and hyperreal artifact, a documentary of images 'without an original referent.' Against Noel Carroll's account of documentary as a film of presumptive assertion and Plantinga's assertive stance, LaRocca shows how Affleck exploited audience faith (staged home movies, the David Letterman 'beat down') so that the film's metaphysical, epistemic and ethical status transformed once the fraud was confirmed. He invokes Hegel's remarks on abstract individuality and compares the case to Herzog's 'ecstatic truth,' Roth's and Kaufman's metafiction, to argue the deception paradoxically discloses deeper truths about what documentary is.

holes.name: Aspect Perception (seeing-as)
holes.what: Wittgenstein's account of 'seeing-as' and the 'dawning of an aspect' (the duck-rabbit), in which perception is inseparably inflected by imagination, concepts and memory.
holes.why: Chapter 30's entire argument that documentary portraiture is truthful turns on aspect-perception specifically, which is distinct from the existing 'language-games' slug and has no dedicated slug.

holes.name: The Film of Presumptive Assertion
holes.what: Noel Carroll's criterion that documentary is defined by the maker's categorical/assertoric intention that the film be taken as asserting something true about the actual world.
holes.why: Chapter 34 (and the volume's recurring frame) depends on this specific concept to explain why a hoax like I'm Still Here betrays documentary expectations; no taxonomy slug names it.
